content: The Joint Committee on Infant Hearing (JCIH) strongly supports the early detection and intervention for infants with hearing loss. The primary objective of Early Hearing Detection and Intervention (EHDI) programs is to optimize linguistic competence and literacy development in children who are deaf or hard of hearing. Without timely opportunities to acquire language, these children are at risk of falling behind their hearing peers in communication, cognitive abilities, reading, and social-emotional development. Such delays can lead to lower educational and employment outcomes in adulthood. To achieve the best outcomes for infants with hearing loss, it is recommended that all infants undergo hearing screening by no later than one month of age. Infants who do not pass the initial screening should receive a comprehensive audiological evaluation by three months of age. Those with confirmed hearing loss should begin appropriate intervention services by six months of age, provided by healthcare and educational professionals with expertise in pediatric hearing loss and deafness. Regardless of the results of initial hearing screenings, all infants should undergo ongoing monitoring of their communicative development starting at two months of age during well-child visits in their medical home. The definition of targeted hearing loss has been expanded to include not only congenital permanent bilateral or unilateral sensory or conductive hearing loss but also neural hearing loss, such as auditory neuropathy/dyssynchrony, particularly in infants admitted to the NICU. Separate screening protocols are recommended for NICU and well-infant nurseries. NICU infants admitted for more than five days should have auditory brainstem response (ABR) testing included in their screening to detect neural hearing loss. Infants who fail automated ABR testing in the NICU should be referred directly to an audiologist for rescreening and, if necessary, a comprehensive evaluation including ABR. For rescreening, a complete assessment of both ears is recommended, even if only one ear failed the initial screening. Infants readmitted to the hospital within the first month of life for conditions associated with potential hearing loss, such as hyperbilirubinemia requiring exchange transfusion or culture-positive sepsis, should undergo repeat hearing screening before discharge. Audiologists with expertise in evaluating newborns and young infants with hearing loss should provide diagnostic audiology services, including auditory habilitation and the selection and fitting of amplification devices. At least one ABR test is recommended as part of a complete audiological evaluation for children under three years of age to confirm permanent hearing loss. The timing and frequency of hearing reevaluations for children with risk factors should be individualized based on the likelihood of delayed-onset hearing loss. Infants who pass neonatal screening but have risk factors should have at least one diagnostic audiology assessment by 24 to 30 months of age. Earlier and more frequent assessments may be necessary for children with conditions such as cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection, syndromes associated with progressive hearing loss, neurodegenerative disorders, trauma, or postnatal infections linked to sensorineural hearing loss. Children who have undergone extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) or chemotherapy, or those with a family history of hearing loss, should also be closely monitored. For families choosing amplification, infants diagnosed with permanent hearing loss should be fitted with an amplification device within one month of diagnosis. Infants with confirmed hearing loss should also be offered a genetics consultation and evaluated by an otolaryngologist with expertise in pediatric hearing loss. Additionally, at least one visual acuity assessment by an experienced ophthalmologist is recommended. All families of infants with any degree of bilateral or unilateral permanent hearing loss should be eligible for early intervention services. Early intervention services should be provided by professionals with expertise in hearing loss, including educators of the deaf, speech-language pathologists, and audiologists. Both home-based and center-based intervention options should be available to families. Regular developmental surveillance, including auditory skills, parental concerns, and middle-ear status, should be conducted in the medical home in accordance with the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) periodicity schedule. Standardized developmental screenings using validated tools should occur at 9, 18, and 24 to 30 months of age, or whenever concerns arise. Infants who fail the speech-language portion of a global screening or for whom there are concerns about hearing or language should be referred for speech-language evaluation and audiology assessment. Parents should receive appropriate follow-up and resource information, and each infant should be linked to a medical home. Information at all stages of the EHDI process should be conveyed to families in a culturally sensitive and understandable format. Families should be informed of all communication options and available hearing technologies in an unbiased manner, with their informed choices guiding the decision-making process. States should implement data-management and tracking systems as part of an integrated child health information system to monitor the quality of EHDI services and provide recommendations for system improvements. The success of EHDI programs depends on families working in partnership with professionals as a well-coordinated team. Essential team members include the birth hospital, families, pediatricians or primary healthcare professionals, audiologists, otolaryngologists, speech-language pathologists, educators of children who are deaf or hard of hearing, and other early intervention professionals. Additional services, such as genetics, ophthalmology, developmental pediatrics, service coordination, and family education, should also be available. Audiologists play a critical role in newborn hearing screening program development, management, quality assessment, and service coordination. Audiologists also provide timely fitting and monitoring of amplification devices and may offer services in educational settings to bridge the gap between families and clinical audiologists. Otolaryngologists specialize in determining the etiology of hearing loss, identifying related risk indicators, and evaluating and treating ear diseases. They assess candidacy for amplification, assistive devices, and surgical interventions, including cochlear implantation, and provide long-term monitoring and follow-up in collaboration with the medical home. Early intervention professionals, trained in disciplines such as speech-language pathology, audiology, and special education, should have specialized expertise in the development of auditory, speech, and language skills. Speech-language pathologists provide evaluation and intervention services for language, speech, and cognitive-communication development. Educators of children who are deaf or hard of hearing integrate communicative competence within various social, linguistic, and academic contexts. Care coordinators are integral members of the EHDI team, facilitating the family’s transition from screening to evaluation to early intervention. They incorporate family preferences into individualized family service plans (IFSPs) and support families in advocating for their child’s developmental needs. The deaf and hard-of-hearing community, including adults and children, can enrich the family’s experience by serving as mentors and role models, providing valuable insights into communication options, assistive technology, and community resources. A successful EHDI program requires collaboration among public and private institutions and agencies responsible for specific components such as screening, evaluation, and intervention.
